newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST-Swedish interest rates seen at bottom.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Swedish interest rates seen at bottom.

text.p: Swedish interest rates have bottomed out and are expected to climb in the short and long term with the spread to Germany still narrowing, according to a monthly Reuters poll of 15 analysts.
Only three of them believed the central bank's key repurchase rate will be cut further from today's level of 4.10 percent.

The majority view was supported by the three most recent statements by the Riksbank, or central bank. Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said as recently as on Thursday there was no need to change the repo rate.
But the analysts forecast on average that the repo rate would stand at 4.22 percent in a year.
Long bond yield rates are also expected to be higher with the ten year bond hovering around 7.50 percent, up from 6.91 percent today.
On a three month horizon a more modest increase was expected with the ten year bond reaching 7.12 percent.
Debt yields were also expected to be driven up by rates internationally in addition to a steadily stronger domestic economy.

"We believe that the Bundesbank will be raising (rates) pretty quickly early in the spring of 1998 and we will follow suit. In addition, the upturn has started here," said Marie Giertz, a Handelsbanken economist.
She expected the repo rate to be at 4.60 percent in a year.
Ake Gustafsson, a Sparbanken economist, also saw a situation where the global interest rate level is rising and where Swedish growth accelerates.

"We see interest rates climbing internationally and the floor will move up," he said. "In Sweden we see gradual growth while inflation won't be high but on the other hand won't be around zero either next year."

Other experts said the Riksbank would rather see too high than too low rates for fear of a return to the inflation policies of old. The Riksbank has several times said it takes time to evaluate the effects of the reductions.

In 1996 the Riksbank cut the repo rate 25 times from a level of 8.91 percent in January to its current level of 4.10 percent. The last repo rate cut was on December 17 when the central bank cut it from 4.35 percent.

Economists forecast the interest rate spread to Germany to narrow to about 112 basis points in a year. In three months the gap was seen around 126 points. At Thursday's close the spread was 117 points.
"The spread is higher now than is called for by fundamentals, and the reason is uncertainty around EMU," Gustafsson said.
He said the gap would narrow as the government's position on EMU, Europe's economic and monetary union, became clear.
"We expect the government to answer a 'soft yes' or a 'soft no' to monetary union," Gustafsson said.
Some economists took the opposite view on the spread.

"We believe it will widen because uncertainty will be even bigger in a year," Giertz said. "We are approaching the election and the EMU scenario is taking shape in Europe while we continue to stand outside."
Handelsbanken saw a spread of 150 basis points in a year against 118 today although the bank believed the government would keep the door for EMU membership open after 1999.
Economists expected the crown to be traded at 4.43 crowns against the mark in a year and at 4.46 crowns in three months compared with 4.4640 crowns on Thursday.
"Several reasons suggest the crown will strengthen and only one suggests why it has not done so yet -- the political distrust in the government," a portfolio manager at an insurance company said.
-- Charlotte Meynert, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1071
